caseno: Appeal From Original Order (FMA).No. 196 of 1996 with Civil Rule 322 (FM) No. 1996.
lawyer:
Shafique Ahmed with MK Rahman, Advocates — For the Appellants.
Aminul Haque, with Abdul Barek Chowdhury, Advocates — For the Respondent No. 1
Khondakar AM Mohsenuddin, Advocate —For the Respondent No. 2
parties:
Magnat Associated Ltd ------ Appellants
Vs. 
GR Textile Mills Ltd ------ Respondent
full_judgment:
2. The appellant as plaintiff filed TS No. 162 of 1996 in the court of Sub-Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka stating, inter alia, that the defendant No. 1 respondent with the financial assistance of the defendant No. 2 respondent purchased machineries and other equipment for setting up a Textile Mill. It has been stated in the plaint that the plaintiff as a local agent of Republic Textile Equipment Co, of South Carolina Incorporated PO Box. 625, 111, Bluckburn Street, York SC 2975, United States of America (hereinafter referred to as the seller) supplied the machineries and equipment to the defendant No. 1 in terms of a contract entered into in between the plaintiff appellant and defendant No. 1 respondent. In terms of the contract an irrevocable documentary credit ie LC, was opened by the defendant No. 1, through defendant No. 2 for a total contracted value of US $ 11,816,500.00 defendant No. 3 respondent as per terms of the contract provided a performance guarantee amounting to US $ 1,816,500.00 in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The seller supplied 80% of the contractual equipment machineries etc. within the extended period of LC, defendant No. 2 took delivery of the machineries and equipments from Chittagong port without any complaint as to their quality, quantity and specification. The plaintiff appellant as local agent of the seller requested the defendant No.1 respondent for extension of the period of LC for supplying the remaining machineries and equipment which have been kept ready but the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respondents with malafide and ulterior motive did not extend the period of LC causing serious loss to the seller as well as to plaintiff appellant. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respondents, unilaterally decreased the value of LC by US$ 3,35,000.00 causing serious loss to the plaintiff appellant and the seller. The seller has fulfilled their, obligation under the contract by supplying machineries, equipment, etc. for the full value of the LC amounting to US $ 1,481,500.00 and the seller is not under any obligation to supply the machineries, equipment for the entire original value of LC as the value of the LC has been reduced. After reduction of the LC value the defendant No. 1 respondent instructed the defendant No. 3 respondent to encash the performance bank Guarantee amounting to US $ 1,816,500.00 causing serious loss to the seller. The seller having duly supplied the equipment, machineries, etc. under the contract to the full value of the amended LC there is no lawful justification for encashment of the performance bank guarantee and the seller is entitled to get back the same. Plaintiff appellant subsequently served notice upon the defendants respondents to settle the dispute through arbitration appointing Mr. Justice Badrul Haider Chowdhury, former Chief Justice of Bangladesh as Arbitrator to resolve the dispute. Defendants respondents without settling the matter through arbitration proceeded illegally to encase the performance bank guarantee. With these allegations the appellant as plaintiff filed the suit for a declaration that the demand made by defendants respondents for encashment of performance bank guarantee amounting to US $ 1816,500.00 is illegal and void. 

 3. After institution of the suit the plaintiff appellant file an application for temporary injunction with a prayer for ad interim-injunction restraining the defendants respondents from encasing the performance bank guarantee. 

 5. It is against this order that the plaintiff as appellant has preferred this appeal contending, inter alia, that the learned Subordinate Judge should have passed an order of ad-interim injunction in considering the facts and circumstances of the case and, as such, the impugned order should be set aside. 

 6. Mr. Shafique Ahmed, learned Advocate for the plaintiff appellant, has submitted that since the seller through their agent, the plaintiff appellant has supplied 80% of the machineries, equipment etc. in terms of the contract and since the matter has been referred to Mr. Justice Badrul Hyder Chowdhury (since dead) former Chief Justice of Bangladesh for arbitration the prayer of the plaintiff appellant for ad-interim injunction should have been allowed and, as such, the impugned order ad interim injunction be passed restraining the defendants respondents from encasing the performance bank guarantee. 

 7. Mr. Aminul Haque, learned Advocate for the defendant-respondent No.1, opposed this appeal asserting that the seller through the plaintiff appellant was required to supply the machineries, equipment, etc. as per specification in terms of the contract as entered into in between the plaintiff appellant and the defendant No.1 respondent and that the supplier through their agent the plaintiff appellant supplied only 49% valued machines as against 80% drawn up value of the LC due to discrepancies in supply, short supply, non-supply and deceitful or fraudulent supply of machines and equipment. He has contended that the machineries, equipment, etc. which were supplied by the seller through this agent the plaintiff appellant were found not according to the specification and that this has been admitted by the plaintiff appellant in the Fax message sent to his principal in Germany on 14th December, 1995 and due to this admission as regards supply of faulty machines, equipment’s etc., the defendants respondents have suffered serious loss and are entitled to encase the performance bank guarantee, He has further contended that this appeal is premature as no order of injunction was passed by the learned Sub-Judge who fixed 31-10-96 for filing WO and for hearing of the injunction matter and, as such, this appeal should be dismissed . He has contended that the court generally does not interfere with commercial transactions and that the Bank issuing letter of Performance Guarantee must pay according to its guarantee unless fraud is noticed and in support of his contention he has cited the case of Uttara Bank vs. Macneill and Kilburn Ltd. and others reported in 1981 BLC (AD) Vol. 1 at page 230. In this case their Lordships have held that the courts are very reluctant to interfere with commercial transactions which have been entered into by the parties in business transactions through performance guarantee or letter of guarantee which are invoked in the commercial dealings and the dispute as to the performance of contract can be resolved by taking resort to appropriate action and the plaintiff if successful would be entitled to damages but certainly not through an order of injunction which would interfere with the normal banking transaction and also contractual obligation of the bank and that the Bank must pay according to its guarantee, on demand, if so stipulated, without proof of conditions except when there is a clear fraud of which the bank has notice. 

 8. Mr. Khandakar AM Mohsenuddin, learned Advocate for the defendant respondent No. 2, has also opposed this appeal and asserted that the LC opened by the defendant No. 1 respondent with defendant No. 1 respondent for purchase of machineries, equipment’s etc. through plaintiff appellant the agent of Republic Textile Equipment Co. of South Carolina made default in supplying the machineries, equipment etc. as per condition laid down in the contract and, as such, there should not be any order of injunction restraining them from encasing the performance bank guarantee. He has further asserted that the defendant No. 2 respondent should not be saddled with financial liability for no fault of their own and that no injunction should be granted restraining them from encasing the performance bank guarantee. 

 9. We have heard the learned Advocates and perused the application for issue of an order of ad-interim injunction including the counter-affidavits, filed on behalf of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respondents. It appears that the defendant No. 1 respondent entered into an agreement with the plaintiff appellant, the local agent of Republic Textile Equipment Co. for supply of machineries, equipment, etc. for setting up a textile mill and for that purpose the defendant No. 2 respondent opened an LC for US $ 1,816,500. It further appears that the plaintiff appellant supplied some machineries, equipment etc. to the defendant No. 1 respondent for setting up a Textile Mill in terms of the contract as entered into in between them. The plaintiff appellant alleged that 80% of the contractual equipment’s, machineries etc. were supplied to the defendant No. 2 respondent and the defendant No. 1 respondent in spite of repeated reminders did not take any step for extension of the period of LC for supplying the remaining machineries, equipment, etc. and finding no other alternative they issued a notice for Arbitration appointing Mr. Justice Badrul Haider Chowdhury, the former Chief Justice of Bangladesh to settle the dispute and that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respondent without taking any step to settle the matter through arbitration with ill motive and also to cause loss to the plaintiff appellant and the seller are trying for encashment of the performance Bank guarantee to their prejudice. Defendant Nos.1 and 2 respondents, on the other hand contended that the supplier through their agent, the plaintiff appellant supplied only 49% valued machines as against 80% drawn up value of the LC due to discrepancies in supply, short supply, non-supply and deceitful or fraudulent supply of machines and equipment, they have contended that the plaintiff appellant has admitted this fault of supplying the machines equipment, etc. which were found not according to specification in a Fax message sent to Mr Helmuth Thelen, THS Nettetal, Germany on 14-12-1995. This Fax message shows that the shipment so far made for supply of the machines, equipment, etc. to the defendant No.1 respondent suffers from some faults which were also verified by the plaintiff respondent by personally checking the machines at the site. In this Fax massage the plaintiff respondent urgently requested the seller to come to Dhaka with a proper technical person to verify the faults, correct them and put them in a running condition. In this Fax message it has also stated that the Bank will take serious legal action against the customer which will ultimately involve the plaintiff respondent and also the seller. 

 10. The learned Advocate for the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respondents in elaborating the faults regarding supply of machines, equipment, etc. on the part of the plaintiff appellant and the seller has contended that no order of injunction should be granted in this case where there are serious faults in the supply of machines, equipment, etc. and that the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 respondents will suffer serious loss if the performance bank guarantee is not encased. In support of this contention they have referred to the decision as already stated above and contended that in this case there is no prima facie case for granting an order of injunction and, as such, the prayer of the plaintiff respondent for ad interim injunction restraining the defendant''s Nos. 1 and 2 respondents from encasing the performance bank guarantee should be rejected. 

 11. It has been decided in the case of Uttara Bank vs. Macneill and Kilburn Ltd. and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 230 that the courts are generally refrained from interfering with commercial transactions in business matter as entered into by the parties through performance guarantee or letter of guarantee which are invoked in the commercial dealings. Of course, the prayer for temporary injunction is granted where there is strong and arguable prima facie case and where the plaintiff will suffer an irreparable loss which cannot be adequately compensated in damage by money or otherwise. In this case the plaintiff respondent alleged to have supplied 80% of the contracted equipment’s, machines etc., which the defendant No. 1 respondent has controverted it stating that 49% of the machines, equipment, etc. as against 80% drawn up value of the LC are supplied. In spite of these claims and counter claims as regards the quantum of machines, equipment’s etc., supplied to the defendant No. 1 respondent, the fact remains that the machines, equipment, etc. so far supplied to the defendant No. 1 respondent by the plaintiff appellant, the agent of Republic Equipment Co. were found not according to the specifications as admitted by the plaintiff appellant in the Fax message sent to Mr. Helmuth Thelen, M/S Nettetal, Germany on 14-12-1995. Further, the learned Subordinate Judge did not pass any order of injunction in the application for temporary injunction with a prayer for ad interim injunction filed by the plaintiff appellant in which there was simply an order for filing written objection by the defendant No. 1 respondent and also for hearing of the injunction matter on 31-10-1996. This appeal against the impugned order appears to be premature as no order was passed by the learned Sub-Judge, in the application for temporary injunction and a date is fixed for hearing of the same. Furthermore, the machineries, equipment, etc. supplied so far by the plaintiff appellant to the defendant No. 1 respondent were found not strictly in conformity with the agreement as entered into in between the plaintiff appellant and defendant No.1 respondent and also not according to appreciation as admitted by the plaintiff appellant in the Fax message which was sent to Mr. Helmuth Thelon in Germany on 14-12-95. In view of this admitted fact and without ascertaining as to what quantum of machineries, equipment, etc. were supplied to the defendant No. 1 respondent by the plaintiff appellant it cannot be said that the plaintiff appellant has been able to make out a prima facie case for granting an order of ad interim injunction. The plaintiff appellant, in our opinion, will not suffer any irreparable loss, injury if an interim injunction is not granted as loss/injury if any, caused to the plaintiff appellant can adequately be compensated in damages by money. Balance of convenience and inconvenience is also not in favour of the plaintiff appellant and, as such, the plaintiff appellants'' prayer for ad interim injunction restraining the defendant Nos.1 and 2 respondents from encasing the performance bank guarantee cannot be considered and it should be rejected.
